 Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 12pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be summarized
by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City Council and will
also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be recorded for
public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Meeting Compensation Disclosure
Pursuant to Government Code Section 54952.3: Disclosure of compensation for meeting
attendance by City Council Members is $790 monthly regardless of the amount of meetings.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items

Agenda Items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including
Ordinances, Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent
Calendar, individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion
of these items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific
items be removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members
of the public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three
(3) minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

  7
 Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers first. After all speakers in the Chambers have spoken,
the Presiding Officer will call upon those participating via zoom or teleconference.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, virtually, email, phone call, mail and any other method which may become
available. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such times when a State of
Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

For the 2022-2023  Program  Year, the City of South Gate (City) received  Community  Development  Block
Grant Program  (CDBG) funds and Home Investment  Partnerships  Program  (HOME) funds to facilitate
accomplishing  the goals set by the  u.s. Department  of Housing and Urban Development  (HUD). As part

resources  made available  during the program  year, accomplishments  based on priorities  established  by
the Consolidated  Plan and documented  in the 2022-2023  Annual Action  Plan, and an assessment  of the
City's annual performance  toward  meeting  its five-year  goals.

The City's mission  is to enhance  the quality  of life for all its residents  by maximizing  the use of available
resources  to assure the availability  of safe, decent,  and affordable  housing. This report  reviews  how the
City achieved  its housing goals by providing  rehabilitation  loans to South Gate homeowners  using HOME
funds. In addition,  how the goals of the non-housing  priorities  of public service programs  were met. All
CDBG funds except for Planning/Administration,  were used for activities  that benefited  low-and-
moderate-income  persons.

HOME Match

As a recipient  of HOME funds, the City is required  to make non-Federal  financial  contributions  to
projects  that qualify  as affordable  housing under the HOME Program.  Annually,  the match contributions
must total a minimum  of 25% of the HOME funds expended  from the City's HOME entitlement  amount
(less administration  costs), unless the City has received  a reduction  in the match requirement.

The HOME statute  provides  for a reduction  of the matching  contribution  requirement  under two
criteria  for fiscal and severe fiscal distress for local PJs:

  1)  Family poverty  rate, and/or
  2)  Per capita  income  (PCI)

When a local jurisdiction  meets one of the distress criteria,  it is determined  to be in fiscal distress and
receives a 50 percent  reduction  of the match.  If a local jurisdiction  satisfies  both distress criteria,  it is
determined  to be in severe fiscal distress and receives a 100 percent  reduction  of the match. The City of
South Gate meets both distress criteria  and, therefore,  receives a 100 percent  reduction  of the match.

The City of South Gate plans, coordinates,  and organizes  strategies  to assist the City's homeless
population  in collaboration  with other public and private  organizations.  The County of Los Angeles,
through  the Los Angeles Homeless  Services Authority  (LAHSA), has the primary  responsibility  for
providing  regional  homeless  services.  Individuals  and families  who do not qualify  as South Gate
residents  are referred  to People Assisting the Homeless  (PATH) for screening  and services intake.

The South Gate Police Department,  in cooperation  with the local Salvation  Army Bell Shelter, operates  a
homeless  outreach  program  that consists of a mobile  outreach  team. The Police Department  Liaison and
personnel  from the Bell Shelter coordinate  street outreach  efforts  by vehicle  and on foot. Street
outreach,  case management,  and referrals  are provided  to homeless  families  and individuals  through
this Program.  Homeless clients are guided  in identifying  barriers to overcoming  homelessness  and
developing  a plan to address these challenges.  The team then assists clients  at a highly supportive  level
to address those needs, including  accessing mainstream  services,  increasing  income, developing  self-
determination,  and accessing shelter  and housing.

Addressing  the emergency  shelter  and transitional  housing  needs  of homeless  persons

provide  both emergency  shelter  and temporary  shelter  to people experiencing  homelessness.  The
shelter  provides  case management  and other  homelessness  services. Homeless  clients are guided  in
identifying  barriers to overcoming  homelessness  and assisted in developing  a plan to overcome  these
barriers.  The team then assists clients at a highly supportive  level to address those needs, including
accessing mainstream  services,  increasing  income,  and developing  self-determination.

Describe  the  standards  and  procedures  used  to monitor  activities  carried  out  in furtherance

At the beginning  of the program  year,  City staff  meets  with  all CDBG and HOME-funded  project

managers  to discuss the reporting  requirements  and the monitoring.  Program  providers  are required  to
provide  progress  reports,  which  are reviewed  for progress  and compliance  at least quarterly.

During  the year,  a site review  is held with  all the program  providers.  An entrance  interview  is held with
key representatives  to review  the program's  purpose,  scope,  objectives,  and goals.  During  the review,

HUD required  records  and  information  is reviewed  and/or collected. The review  ends with  an exit
conference  to present  preliminary  results  of the monitoring,  this provides  an opportunity  to discuss
program  compliance  and reporting  concerns.  At this point,  the program  provider  can also share  steps to
address  non-compliance  or non-performance  areas.  Formal  notification  of the monitoring  review
results  is sent to the program  provider,  which  creates  a permanent  written  record,  an outline  of any

concerns  and/or findings, and sets deadlines for a written response  and corrective  actions.  The Monitor
is responsible  for providing  technical  assistance  to ensure  the programs  are productive  and compliant
with  federal  regulations.  Staff continuously  monitors  programs  and activities  to comply  with  city, state,
and federal  regulations  and policies  with  a focus  on:

  *  Financial  Standards  and Procedures  - Community  Development  staff and the City's  accounting
  division  work  closely  to ensure  funds  drawn  through  IDIS are used for authorized  activities  on
  approved  projects.  Activity  agreements,  expense  documentation,  and approvals  must  be in
  place before  expending  funds.

  *  Environmental  Standards  and Procedures  - All projects  and individual  activities  requiring

  Bnvironmental  reviews  per HUD regulations  are completed  before  funding  approval.  Staff
  completed  the appropriate  Environmental  Reviews  for all CDBG and HOME  programs.

  *  Labor Standards  and Procedures  - Community  Development,  Public Works  staff,  and outside

  consultants  monitor  labor  standards.  Labor requirements  are included  in all bid documents  and
  reviewed  again during  the pre-construction  meeting.

  departments)  to submit  quarterly  performance  reports  and requests  for reimbursements.  Upon

  from  the service  and compare  it to the subrecipient's  goals for the program.  Staff also review  all

During  monitoring  for HOPE Housing,  it was found  that four  (4) tenants  did not have sufficient  source

staff  requested  that  the property  management  provide  all missing  documentation.  During  the
monitoring  visit staff were  informed  that there  was a change  in property  management  companies,  from
the previous  fiscal year, staff spoke  at length  and reminded  the property  management  of the program
requirements  while  referring  them  to helpful  tools  and resources.

found  that  two  (2) unites  needed  minor  repairs  which  the property  management  team  addressed.  As

 SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  DECLARING  A CONTINUED  EMERGENCY  AND
 AUTHORIZING  REPAIR,  REPLACEMENT  OR MAINTENANCE  ACTIVITIES  OF
 PUBLIC  FACILITIES  RELATED  TO THE URBAN ORCHARD,  CITY PROJECT  NO.
 539-PRK  WITHOUT  PUBLIC  BIDDING,  PURSUANT  TO  THE  EMERGENCY
 CONTRACTING  PROCEDURES  OF THE SOUTH  GATE MUNICIPAL  CODE AND
 THE CALIFORNIA  PUBLIC CONTRACT  CODE

PURPOSE:  To declare an emergency still exists and to authorize the repair, replacement or
maintenance activities of public facilities related to the Urban Orchard Project without public
bidding.  The Los Angeles County Department  of Public Health, Solid Waste Division
("County")  issued a Corrective Action Order requiring construction to stop on the project. The
declaration of emergency is necessary to streamline the process to procure a replacement
contractor to provide maintenance activities to preserve the site in a safe condition until the
County authorizes construction work on the project to resume.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider making a finding and adopting
a Resolution  declaring an emergency still exists and authorizing  repair, replacement or
maintenance activities of public facilities related to the Urban Orchard, City Project No. 539-
PRK, without public bidding, pursuant to the emergency contracting procedures of the South
Gate Municipal Code and the California Public Contract Code.

FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. The Urban Orchard Project
("Project") has received a total of $30.5 million in grant and other funds for design, construction,
operations, and maintenance, as summarized below, inclusive of a $5,000,000 grant from
 Caltrans.

ANALYSIS:  The Project was under construction and approximately 80% of construction work
has been completed. On December 29, 2022, the City received a Corrective Action Order
("Order") from the County. The Order required the City to stop all construction activities until
such time as a Post Closure Land Use Plan ("PCLUP")  for the Project site was approved by the
County. Given the PCLUP approval process and input received to date, it will take at least
several months, possibly six or more, to obtain approval.

  1  46
 To  avoid  the  significant  delay  damages  that  would  be payable  by  the  City  to the  general
contractor  during  a proloriged  suspension  of the project  pending  approval  of the PCLUP,  the City
Council  terminated  the general  contractor's  agreement  at a Special  City  Council  meeting  on
February  6, 2023.  Such termination  provided  both  immediate  and long-term  cost savings  to the
City  but also created  an immediate  need for the City  to retain  an interim  contractor  to perform
certain  ongoing  maintenance  and safety  activities;  a need which  must  be met  sooner  than  the
time necessary  to engage  in normal  public  bidding  procedures

The proposed  Resolution  declares  a continued  emergency  exists pursuant  to the authority  granted
by South Gate Municipal Code F3 l.54.470 and California Public Contract Code '8322050. Those
Code  Sections  allow  cities,  by resolution,  to approve  the  City's  entry  into  contracts  without
engaging  in public  bidding  where  certain  emergency  conditions  are found  to have occurred.  Staff
continues  to believe  that the County's  Order  directing  all construction  work  to be ceased on the
Project,  constitutes  such an emergency  due to the public's  safety  with  an unfinished  construction
site and the need to respond  accordingly  to additional  directives  given  by the County  related  to
ensuring  public  safety.  Staff  is  recommending  that  the  City  Council  adopt  the  proposed
Resolution  so that the City  can avail  itself  of the accelerated  contracting  procedures  authorized
by those  Code  Sections.  The  Resolution,  (1)  declares  an emergency,  (2)  authorizes  the  City
Manager  to take  such  actions  deemed  necessary  to  cause  the  maintenance  activities  to  be
performed  and to procure  the necessary  equipment,  services,  and supplies  all without  giving
notice  for bids for contracts,  (3) requires  that at each regularly  scheduled  City  Council  Meeting,
the City  Manager  present  to the  Council  the reasons  justifying  why  the emergency  will  not
permit  a delay  resulting  from  a competitive  solicitation  for bids, why  that action  is necessary  to
respond  to the emergency,  and that the City  Council  review  the emergency  action  to determine,
by a four-fifth's  vote,  that there is a need to continue  the emergency  action  until  the emergency
action  is terminated.

The  City  is working  diligently  to secure  the PCLUP  approval.  The process  has been  initiated
with  the submittal  of technical  documents  such  as the Workplan  for  interim  measures  and a
Summary  of Site Investigation,  and the City  continues  to address  the requirements  imposed  by
the County.

Since  the original  Resolution  declaring  an emergency  was  approved  by the  City  Council  on
February  6, 2023, the following  contracts,  expenditures,  and milestones  have been undertaken:

  1,  NR Development  Inc., was informed  that Contract  No. 2021 -66-CC  was terminated  by
  the City  Council  effective  February  13, 2023,  except  for maintenance  activities.  Staff
  met with  NR Development  Inc., to discuss  the steps to close out construction  activities
  and continue  maintenance  activities.  As of February  16, 2023, NR Development  Inc., is
  no longer  providing  any project  services  or maintenance  activities.

  2.  City  forces  are providing  maintenance  services  of the site. The site has been secured
  with  perimeter  fencing  and security  contract  services.

  3.  Coordination  with  the  Trust  for  Public  Land  ("TPL")  to  complete  the  process  to
  prepare  the technical  documents  necessary  to  secure  a replacement  contractor  was

   completed. Preliminarily  selected a recommended interim contractor; conducted a field
  review; and received a fee proposal for the interim maintenance and construction
  activities approved by the Local Enforcement Agency ("LEA").  Received a proposal
  from the contractor and have begun negotiations.

  4.  Submitted to the LEA the Summary of Investigations Report, Workplan of Interim
  Control Measures ("WICM"),  Supplemental WICM and Phase II Workplan. Received
  approval of the WICM and conditional approval of the Phase II Workplan. Submitted  a

  5.  Approved a funding increase for TPL in the amount of $50,000. On January 24, 2023,
  the City Council approved a $250,000 budget for z"unendment  No. 6 to Contract No.

  budget increase of $50,000 was administratively  approved to align the amount of the
  budget authority with the $300,000 budget requirement for Amendment No. 6, which
  provides funding for the technical services required to comply with requirements  from
  the LEA.

  6.  A bid was received from LA Engineering to complete the construction of maintenance
  activities in the WICM approved by the LEA for the Urban Orchard Project. A
  construction contract in the amount of $2,919,248 was executed administratively  under

  anticipates completing the work in December  2023.

BACKGROUND:  The Project is a part of the FY 2022/23 Capital Improvement Program. The
Project is located between the Los Angeles River, Firestone Boulevard, the Thunderbird Villa
Mobile Home Park, and the I-710 Freeway. Two primary purposes of the Project are to divert
and treat storm water run-off from the Los Angeles River and provide recreation opportunities to
South  Gate residents.

The Project is being constructed on a property that was used as an unpermitted landfill until 1949
by an entity known as Southeastern Disposal and By-Products. The property site is identified  in
CalRecycle's Solid Waste Information System ("SWIS") as an Unpermitted Closed Solid Waste
Disposal Site and SWIS No. 19-AA-5545. In 1984, the State of California Department of Health
Services, Toxic Substances Control Division  concluded that the clean-up work completed
effectively  mitigated  waste constituents  to proceed with the Lewis Homes residential
development project. The requirements of the PCLUP came into effect in 1988. As such, the
project site is subject to State solid waste regulations that require the PCLUP before any change
to the current land use, construction, or land preparation  can occur.

The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, Solid Waste Management Program,  acts
as the LEA for the State of California's Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
("CalRecycle"). The County is authorized by Division  30 of the Public Resources Code

  3
  48
 ("PRC"),  Section  43209  and 45000,  Title  14 and 27 of the California  Code  of Regulations  (14
CCR  & 27 CCR),  to enforce  applicable  solid  waste  regulations  and to ensure  solid  waste  sites
meet  the  state  minimum  standards  within  the  County  of Los  Angeles.  As  such,  the  City  is
working  with  the LEA  to obtain  approval  of the PCLUP.

Construction  is  currently  at  the  80%  completion  stage.  Improvements  that  have  been
substantially  completed  include,  but are not limited  to, rough  grading,  drop inlet  for storm  water
diversion  structures  in the Bandini  Channel,  a wetland  overlook  area, the stream  adjacent  to the
education/flexible  space  building  and  wetland,  south  bio  swale,  construction  of  18  raised
planters,  planting  of  75  trees,  installation  of  the  prefabricated  education  center  and  the
restroorn/maintenance  building,  two  shade  structures,  a water  element  at the  playground,
installation  of multi-use  walking  and bicycle  pathways,  exercise  equipment  located  at various
stages along  the walking  and bicycle  paths, benches,  picnic  tables,  drinking  fountains,  trash cans,
and pathway  lighting. The total estimated cost of improvements  completed  to date is over  $12
million.

The Project  has received  the listed  grants.  The process  has begun  to enter into an agreement  with
Caltrans  to receive  an additional  $5 million  for a grand total of $30.5 million.

  PURPOSE:  To approve  and adopt  a comprehensive  pay schedule  for all full-time,  part-time,
  and  elected  officials  within  the  Califomia  Public  Employee  Retirement  System  (CalPERS)
  guidelines.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City  Council  will  consider  adopting  a Resolution  amending
 Resolution  No. 6454 (Salary  Resolution  and Position  Classification  Plan) to approve  and adopt  a
  comprehensive  pay schedule  for all full-time,  part-time,  and elected  officials  within  the CalPERS
 guidelines.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact.

 ANAI,YSIS:  None.

 BACKGROUND:  CalPERS,pursuanttoitsinterpretationoftheCaliforniaCodeofRegulations
 § 570.5  of the Public  Employees'  Retirement  Law  (PERL),  as outlined  in its January  8, 2020
 Circular  Letter,  recommends  that all CalPERS  employers  maintain  their  compensation  levels  in
 one publicly  available document,  approved  and adopted  by the governing  body,  which  must meet
 all of the following  criteria:
  1)  Hasbeendulyapprovedandadoptedbytheemployer'sgoverningbodyinaccordancewith
  the requirements  of applicable  public  meetings  laws;
  2)  Identifies  the position  title  for every  employee  position;
  3)  Shows the pay rate for each identified  position,  which  may be stated as a single  amount  or
  as multiple amounts within a range;
  4)  Indicates  the time base, including,  but not limited  to, whether  the time base is hourly,  daily,
  bi-weekly,  monthly,  bi-monthly,  or annually;
  5)  Is posted  at the office  of the employer  or immediately  accessible  and available  for public
  review  from  the employer  during  normal  business  hours  or posed  on the  employer's
  internet  website;

  1

  53
   6)  Indicates  an effective  date and date of any revisions;
  7)  Is retained by the employer  and available  for public  inspection  for not less than five years;
  and
  8)  Does not reference  another document  in lieu of disclosing  the pay rate.

Effective the first full pay period of July 2023, the City's full-time employees received
  a negotiated
pay increase contained  eitlier in their respective Memorandum  of Understanding  or in an
agreement. Additionally,  several of the part-time hourly positions that have corresponding  full-
time equivalents also received a pay increase to keep the positions in parity.

Under the PERL and the Public Employees' Pension Refori'n Act of 2013 (PEPRA),
  compensation
 earnable and pensionable compensation are determined in accordance with the
  amounts identified
 on a publicly available pay schedule as adopted and approved by the City Council.
  If an employer
were to fail to meet with requirements of Section 570.5 as stated above, the
  CalPERS Board may
deten'nine at its sole discretion an amount that will be considered as a pay rate
  in determining what
a retiree's eamable income will be, which will never be higher than the amount
  stated on the
comprehensive  salary schedule. As a result, publicly  available pay schedules are required by
CalPERS and are a critical component to verify all members' pay rates when calculating
  members'
retirement benefits. Finally, maintaining  a compliant publicly available pay schedule will support
transparency and expedite CalPERS' review process. Failure to provide CalPERS
  with a compliant
publicly available pay schedule may result in a retirement benefit being delayed
  and/or reduced.

Therefore,  the purpose of approving  this resolution is to combine the City's various payroll
schedules into a single schedule for approval by the City Council. It is the staff's intent
  to continue
to produce a single schedule going forward for both CalPERS and City purposes
  at the time any
salary schedule is revised.

  Annual  Business  Meeting/General  Assembly  where  membership  considers  and  acts  on
  resolutions  that  establish  Cal Cities'  policy.  These  resolutions  guide  cities  and the League  in
  their  efforts  to  improve  the  quality,  responsiveness,  and  vitality  of  local  government  in
  California.  Each member  city has the right  to cast one vote on matters pertaining  to the League
  of California  Cities  policies  that are being  considered by the General Assembly.

  Historically,  the City  has designated  the two  City  Council  Members  who  serve as delegate  and
  alternate  to the LA  County  Division  of the League  of California  Cities.  At present,  those two
  members  are Mayor  Maria  del Pilar  Avalos  who would  represent  the City  as the voting  delegate
  and Vice  Mayor  Gil Hurtado  who would  serve as the first  alternate  delegate.

  voting  delegates  to vote and take action  during  the Annual  Conference  and Expo.  The proposed
  Resolution  designates  Mayor  Avalos  as the  voting  delegate.  Vice  Mayor  Hurtado  is not
  attending  the conference  so Council  Member  Davila  is being  proposed  to represent  the City  as
  the alternate  voting  delegate  and Council  Member  Rios  is be proposed  as the second  alternate

 ANALYSIS:  Mark  Thomas  & Company,  Inc.,  ("Mark  Thomas")  was  awarded  Contract  No.
3563  to  provide  design  services  which  primarily  entail  the  preparation  of  the  plans,
specifications,  estimates  and construction  support  services  for the Long  Beach  Boulevard  Street
Improvements  Project,  City  Project  No.  515-ST,  Federal  Project  Nos.  ATPL-5257(033)  and
HSIPL-5257(037)  (Project).  Amendment  No.  2 provides  an extension  of  the  term  through
December  31,  2024,  to  allow  time  to  complete  construction  and  close  out  the  Project.
Amendment  No.  2 also  funds  services  that  were  needed  to finalize  the  design  plans  which
included  funds  for median  modification  ($11,502), bioswale relocation ($15,204), traffic control
changes  ($15,401),  bid package  revision  ($10,978) to meet budget requirements,  and the final
construction  plan set revision  ($14,430).

BACKGROUND:  The  Project  is a part  of the Capital  Improvement  Program.  It proposes
safety,  traffic  circulation,  landscaping  and greening  and beautification  improvements  from  Santa
Aria Street to Tweedy  Boulevard.

On November  26, 2019,  the City  Council  approved  Contract  No. 3563 with  Mark  Thomas  in the
amount  of $664,592  to provide  engineering  plans,  specifications  and estimates  for the Project.

On August  24, 2021,  the City  Council  approved  Amendment  No.  I with  Mark  Thomas  in the
amount  of $67,850  to provide  additional  services  inclusive  of a traffic  study,  preliminary  tree
risk  assessment,  Right-of-Way  Certification  and construction  permit  as required  by  Caltrans.
Amendment  No.  l  also  provided  for  an extension  of  the  term  of  the  agreement  through
December  31, 2023.

Construction  began on September  11, 2023, and is scheduled  to be completed  in April  2023.

The  vision  for  Long  Beach  Boulevard  is to transform  the  corridor  into  an attractive  urban
environment  with  a diverse  mix  use. This will  require  a significant  complete  streets improvement
program  that  includes  greening  the  corridor  with  energy  efficient  systems,  storm  water
infiltration  planters,  improved  traffic  circulation  and  safety,  promoting  alternative  modes  of
transportation  with  enhanced  pedestrian  mobility  and bike  amenities,  an enhanced  streetscape
environment  and  other  pedestrian  environment  enhancements.  More  specifically,  project
amenities  include  raised  landscaped  median  islands  with  drought  tolerant  vegetation;  vegetated
bio-filtration  swales;  storm  water  capture,  treatment  and  infiltration;  roadway  pavement
rehabilitation  and restriping;  high  visibility  enhanced  crosswalks  and rectangular  rapid  flashing
beacons;  sidewalk  repairs  and ADA  compliant  curb ramps;  bike  racks  and striping  for class III
bicycle  facilities.  These  elements  have  safety,  transportation,  beautification,  and quality  of life
benefits.

  TASK1 - MEDIAN  UPLIGHTING

  The City requested  uplighting  on the median  island trees  be included  as part of the design
  package.  Original  scope  of services  only included  parkway  lighting.  Efforts  included  the
  design,  electrical  load calculations  and plan preparation  for the uplighting.  Please note that
  this additional  effort  was approved  by the City as per your email dated September14,  2021.

  Taskl  Estimated  Cost:  $2,500

  TASK2-MEDIAN  ISLAND/LEFTTURN  POCKETMODIFICATIONS

  As part of Change  Order  No.1, a traffic  analysis was prepared  for the left turn queuing
  capacities  to validate  the storage  lengths  were adequate.  As an outcome  of that analysis,
  median  island modifications  were required  to lengthen  multiple  turn pockets.  This effort
  included  revised  horizontal  layout,  updating  layout  plans and callouts,  quantities  and cost
  estimates,  planting,  irrigation  and hardscape  layouts.

  Task 2 Estimated  Cost:  $9,002

  TASK 3 - BIOSWALE RELOCATION TO PARKWAY

  preparation  of the100%  plans, the City  requested  that  the bioswales  be located  in the

  bioswales,  creation  of additional  bioswales  to ensure  near-equal  treatment  as originally
  planned,  revised  bioswale  details  to accommodate  the sidewalk,  updated  grading

  calculations,  revised  civil  layout,  planting  and irrigation  plans, quantity  calculations  and
  estimates.

  TASK 4 - DECORATIVE  SIDEWALK

  Per the  ATP grant,  enhanced  crosswalks  were  proposed  at several  locations.  Through  the
  90% completion  of the project  plans, these  were  identified  as a painted,  stamped  asphalt
  pattern  crosswalk  on the civil layout  sheets.  The City  subsequently  provided  direction  to
  use colored,  stamped  concrete  crosswalks,  which  were  incorporated  into the project

  design  and shown  on the civil,  signing  and striping,  construction  staging,  planting  and
  median  plans.  Construction  details  were  added.  Following  the draft100%  plan submittal  for
  the grant  funding,  the City  requested  that  these  concrete  crosswalks  be removed  and to
  use high visibility  continental  crosswalks  instead.  As requested,  all of the above  project
  plans,  quantities  and estimate  were  updated  accordingly.

  Task 4 Estimated  Cost:  $2,915

  TASK 5 - CONSmUCTION  STAGING/mAFFIC  HANDLING

  Up through  the  90% submittal,  the project  plans reflected  a construction  staging/traffic

  handling  approach  of maintaining  one lane of travel  in each  direction  along  with  on-street
  parking.  Prior  to the draft100%  plan submittal,  the City  requested  that  two  lanes be

  maintained,  particularly  during  rush hour.  In order  to provide  the two  lanes and sufficient

  room  to construction  the median  improvements,  parking  would  have to be eliminated.  As
  such,  the City  further  requested  to limit  the  length  of no-parking  to a reasonable  distance,
  discussed  to be approximately  two  blocks  in length  at any point  in time.  The construction

  staging/traffic  handling  sheets  were  completely  overhauled  to incorporate  this request.

  TASK 6 - BID PACKAGE  CHANGES

  Following  the submittal  of the bid ready plans, specification  and estimate,  the City
  recognized  that the estimate  exceeded  the available  budget  and requested  the bid additive
  alternatives  be included  so that the base bid would  remain  under the available  budget.  This
  resulted  in significant  cost analysis and comparison  with the grant funding,  developing
  alternative  scenarios  to reduce  the project  base cost and included  an additional  detailed
  field review  over a weekend  to develop  alternative  a Tier 1 and Tier 2 approach  to the
  sidewalk,  curb and gutter  and access ramps. Ultimately  a PDF set of drawings  were marked
  up for bidding  purposes  and the bid schedule  and project  specifications  modified  to reflect
  seven bid additive  alternates.

  Since joining  the project  in July 2021, at no time did the City indicate  an issue with the
  project  cost estimate  related  to the City's  budget.  A few items of note:

  *  The project  exceeded  the City budget  dating  back to the 90% submittal  in October
  2020.  There was no mention  of the budget  being a concern,  including  the
  estimates  that had been provided  through  the bid ready submittal,  until the project
  went to bid.

  City staff  provided  direction  during  a field review  in early 2021 for the removal  and
  replacement  limits of sidewalk  and curb and gutter.  These limits and quantities
  were reflected  in the Bid Peady plans. These quantities  still far exceeded  the
  quantities  included  in the ATP and HSIP grant funding.

  The grant funding  applications  for ATP, HSIP and Green  Streets  grossly
  underestimated  the quantity  and unit costs for the actual  work required  to
  construct  the improvements  depicted  in those  applications.

  ,  Construction  market  volatility  has continued  since 2020,  with a significant  increase

  in costs for which  Mark Thomas  cannot  be held responsible  for.

PROJECT  UNDERSTANDING
Long Beach Boulevard is a five-lane, 70-foot wide heavily traveled auto-oriented primary arterial traversing
north-south through the City. The corridor stretches 1.5 miles from the Tweedy Boulevard intersection in the
south to Santa Ana Street in the north and includes on-street parking. Sidewalks along the corridor range from
4- to 15-feet wide and several blocks have existing street trees. Also, within the sidewalks are street lights and
overhead utility poles. The facility currently lacks bicycle facilities and many of the intersections lack modern
crosswalks and ADA-compliant curb ramps.

The heavy automobile use along the corridor has
resulted in traffic congestion and deterioration of
the pavement. Long Beach Boulevard has an ADT
of 25,000 vehicles. There are also closely spaced
intersections and multiple driveways that, along
with the ADT, contribute to the impact in trafflc
operations. Pavement along Long Beach Boulevard
consists oF concrete pavement and asphalt
concrete. The wear from the heavy traffic and
age of the pavement has resulted in the need for
rehabilitate the pavement.

Long Beach Boulevard is a critical corridor to the
community. There are local businesses and other
points of interest, such as more than10 scliool,
multiple commercial centers, and several churches
along and in close proximity to the corridor. There  Lotig tEecichBoui'evord Existing Coridittoris
are also residential land uses close to the corridor as well.

The combination of land uses, existing conditions, and multimodal users has resulted in conflicts along Long
Beach Boulevard. From 2007 to 2017, there have been 231 collisions along the corridor. Of the total crashes,
there has been one fatality and 21 pedestrian-involved crashes. The vehicle collisions involve broadsides, head-
ons, and rear ends as a result oF stopped vehicles and left turns from the center turn lane.

The City's 2035 General Plan recognizes the need to improve Long Beach Boulevard to make it rnultimodal
friendly. The general plan recommends improving the streetscape, enhancing 5he pedestrian environment,
and install medians. These efforts will support the long-term economic development goals for the corridor to
provide medium and high-density mixed use creating an attractive urban environment.

The City has successfully secured multiple funding sources to design and construct improvements to the
corridor to address safety and multimodal deficiencies, improve pavement condition, reduce ti-affic congestion,

seeking additional funds for the project. This includes funds through the 1-710 Technical Advisory Committee,

concrete is in good-to-fair  condition and the asphalt concrete in poor condition wjth a highly aged (cracked)

recommendations  forthe  City, we will perform  an initial visual assessment,  perform  non-destructive  testing,
perform a ground  penetrating  radar (GPP) assessment, and complete  a geotechnicat  investigation  and testing  of

*  Warm Mix Asphalt  (WMA) pavement  overlays

* Alternative rehabilitation methods (in-place  recycling,  mill and fill treatments)

Drainage  and Green  Infrastructure
Streets  present  both a barrier  to stormwater  run-off  and an opportunity
for a better  approach  to stormwater  management.  By applying  practices
set forth  in the "Green  Street  Municipal  Handbook",  a focused  design
can address  water  quality  treatment  along with the traffic  calming  and
safety  benefits  or a physical  buffer.  Biofiltration  designs  require  a unique
in-depth  knowledge  of drainage,  soil, and plant material  for a lasting,  and
functional  feature.

Roadway  Drainage
The storm  drainage  of Long Beach Boulevard  relies on very few inlets at
collection  areas near large intersections,  storm  water  typically  crossed
cross streets  via cross gutters.  Flooding  during  medium  to intense  storm
events  are common  in the area due to the lack of drainage  inlets.

The existing  storm  drainage  pattern  Will not be modified  with the project,
however  there  are project  improvements  that can improve  drainage  and
relieve  the overtaxed  existing  drainage  system.  The flooded  width  can
be reduced  by increasing  the cross slope on flat areas of the road to
concentrate  the storm  water  and minimize  wide flooding  or the roadway.

The proposed  bio-swales  and green elements  of the project  will reduce  the amount  of storm  runoff  that reaches
the exis'ting  storm  drain syste,m. The green  infrastructure  of the project  is discussed  in the next section.

The soil of the biofiltration  planter  is integral  to its success  in treating  stormwater  runoff  and the long-term
health  oF plantings.  These criteria  result  in specific  import  soil requirements  that make the soil difficult  to source.
If not researched  and specified  correctly  in the design  phase, these  sourcing  issues can result in project  delays
and/or  change  orders  during  construction.  We have developed  a database  of suppliers  that meet  the strict
specifications  of the required  soil medium.  We understand  from  our early research  of the project  that the base
existing  soil along  Long Beach  Boulevard  has high infiltration  rates. These existing  sandy and foamy soils acting  as
a base upon which  the bioretention  soil will be placed  will successfully  handle  a bioretention  usage provided  we
use the appropriate  plant materials.

While the plants  from  the proposed  Long Beach  Boulevard  palette  in
the Urban  Greening  Grant  application  are appropriate  for a typical
streetscape  condition,  some  plants listed would  be challenged  to
establish  and survive  long term  within  a bioretention  setting.  Plants
used in this condition  must be adapted  to handle  the periodic
inundation  and seasonally  wet conditions  while maintaining  a low water
use profile  and a tolerance  for high winds (caused  by passing vehicles)
and the heat island effect  of the street  environment.  This also applies
to any trees planted  within  a low impact  development  area. Proposed
trees must tolerate  similar  conditions  as specified  shrubs  and grasses
and have a non-invasive  root  system.  Our team of in-house  landscape
architects  will develop  a plant  palette  that addresses  the challenges  of
a successful  establishment  within  the planting  areas regardless  of their
function.

Authorization  Processing

Assistance.  We are knowledgeable  of the federal  and/or  state  laws,
regulations,  policies  and procedures  related  to design,  right  of way
certification,  utility  coordination,  construction  and maintenance.  Federal

preparing  RFAs and supporting  information  for the various  project  phases,
preparing  Right-of-Way  and Utility  Certification  Forms  and submitting  and
receiving  approval  for PS&E.

 Construction,  Inc., submitted the only bid in the amount of $280,480. Staff is recommending
proceeding  to award a construction  contract. Rebidding the project would delay construction
:[urther and could result in higher bids as construction pricing continues to increase.

To date, the City Council has appropriated $135,200 to the project inclusive  of $17,600  in
LAUSD  Escrow funds, and $117,600 in Measure W. Appropriations  of $87,880  in Measure  W
and $222,718  in LAUSD Funds are needed to 'fully fund construction  equaling  a total proposed
funding  of $310,598 and a total proposed budget of $445,798.

BACKGROUND:  The Project is part of the City's Capital Improvement  Program. The Project
entails construction of two catch basins and stormwater infiltration  units, street light conduit,
sidewalk, curb ramps, curb and gutter, and tree removals.

On July 19, 2023, staff advertised  the Notice Inviting Bids for construction in the Daily Journal.
The Project was also advertised  on the City's website. On August 10, 2023, two bids were
received  and opened by the City Clerk in a public forum. The summary of the bids is as follows:

  Contractor  Base Bid
  Bali  Construction,  Inc.  $280,480
  Axiom  Group  $398,187

Staff recommends  awarding  the Base Bid in the amount of $280,480.

Bali  Construction,  Inc., is based in South El Monte, California.  The company has been in
business  for over 35 years. Staff contacted listed references and received positive commentary.
The company has the capacity and experience to perform the work required under the bid
solicitation.

The City Council is requested to authorize the City Manager to administratively  approve change
orders up to $75,000. This will accelerate project changes to avoid delays in payment or delays
in the construction schedule.

Pursuant to the guidelines of the California  Environmental  Quality Act (CEQA), this Project is
categorically exempt under Title 14 of the California  Code of Regulations, Section 15301, Class
I(b) exemption for replacement for public utility services.

Construction  is scheduled to begin in September 2023. The procurement  lead time is estimated  to
be 4-6 weeks. It is anticipated that the Project will be completed in January 2024.

  of the Sewer Lining Project.  The repairs were

  pipelines.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:
  The City Council will consider authorizing  the AsSistant City
  Manager/Director  of Public
  Works to approve Change Order No. 3 to Contract
  No. 2022-105-CC
  with Southwest  Pipeline and Trenchless  Corporation  to :tund emergency  repairs that were
  necessary to complete the construction of the Sewer
  Lining Project, City ProjectNo.  629-SWR, in
  the amount of $36,000.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. Change
  Order No. 3 is in the
 amount  of $36,000  and will be funded with Sewer Funds. The project

 below:

 ANALYSIS:  The project  was implemented  to reline sewer pipelines. After construction  began,
 the contractor  conducted  a CCTV inspection  and found severe degradation  of pipelines  on

  1  193
   California  Avenue  and on the alley  north  of Abbott  Road.  Construction  could not continue until
  the pipeline  segments  were repaired.  Emergency  repairs  were completed  at a total cost of $36,000.
  This was an unforeseen  field  condition  which  required  compensating  the contractor  for extra work.

  Change  Order
  No. 3 requires City Council approval to meet
  the requirements  of Section 1.54.610
  Approval  of Modification  and Change Orders (E) of the South Gate
  Municipal  Code. This section
 requires City Council  approval of change orders for contracts having
  an original  contract amount
 equal to or greater than fifty thousand dollars
  which modification  (individually  or together with
 any previous modification)  increases the total amount ofthe city's obligations
  by more thantwenty
 percent (20%).

 BACKGROUND:  The  Sewer Lining  Project is budgeted  in the Fiscal Year 2022/23  Capital
 Improvement  Program.  The improvements  include the application  of a cure-in-place liner to sewer
 mains  and manholes  on California Ave and on the alley north of Abbott Road.

 On November  10, 2022,  the City  awarded  construction  Contract  No. 2022-105-CC  to Southwest
 Pipeline  and Trenchless  Corporation  in the amount  of $89,950.

 On February  21, 2023, the City approved Change Order
  No. I for $3,640. The change order was
 needed  to increase the thickness  of the materials that were installed to line the pipelines. This
 procedure  provides  for durability,  and a more structurally  sound product  that has a 50-year
 lifetime.

 On April 10, 2023, the City approved Change Order
  No. 2 in the amount of $2,160. The change
order  was needed to increase the diameter  of the liner from 10-inch  to 12-inch to match the
diameter of the pipeline found on California
  Avenue.

A'Jter  construction  began,  the  contractor  encountered  unforeseen  field  conditions.  A  video
inspection  of  the  pipelines  found  issues  warranting  emergency  repairs  prior  to  completing
constructiori.  The pipelines  could  not be relined  until  the interior  pipe conditions  were repaired.

Construction  of the project  is now  complete.

 CITY  COUNCIL  QUARTERLY  BRIEFING

 PURPOSE:  The
  City of South Gate was awarded a $500,000  U.S. Environmental  Protection
 Agency  (EPA)  Brownfields  Cornmunitywide  Assessment  Grant to assess properties that could be
 cleaned  up and redeveloped  to meet the City's economic  and housing goals.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider  the following  actions:
  a.  Receive  and file.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  Funding  for the citywide  brownfields  assessment would  come  from  the
 City's  allocation  of the US EPA  2023 Communitywide  Brownfields  Assessment  Grant.  There  is
 no impact  on the General  Fund.

ANALYSIS:  This  project  supports  the  City  Council's  goals  of "encouraging  economic
development"  and  "development  and  protecting  strong,  sustainable  neighborhoods."  To
implement  the City's  Economic  Development  Strategy
  and affordable  housing goals, the City is
looking  to identify  all potential
  sites that hazardous materials may impact in the City's
  commercial
and industrial  areas and affordable  housing sites identified  in the Housing Element.

The Grant  provides  :tunding  to inventory
  the larger target areas, and based upon a prioritization
methodology,  to characterize,  assess, and conduct cleanup planning  on a limited number of high-
potential  revitalization  housing sites. The results will include an assessment
  of the properties in
the revitalization  investment  areas and identi:ty and prioritize  the sites that will achieve the City's
economic reinvestment  objectives.  To support the implementation  of the Grant, the EPA requires
the development  and implementation  of a local Community  Engagement  Plan ("CEP").  The CEP
will help the public  understand  the EPA Brownfields  Assessment  process and help the City
identify  community  priorities  for near and long-term  cleanup and reuse of brownfield  sites.

The  community  engagement  consultant,  Craig  Communications,  SCS Engineers,  the company
conducting  the brownfields  assessment,  RSG,  the  City's  partner  in managing  the  grant,  and
volunteer  community  partners  will  work  together  to inform  South  Gate residents  and business

 owners of Grant's goals and objectives and obtain community feedback
  on how best to prioritize
sites for economic and housing development. The team will also provide
  ongoing communications
on the progress and results of this effort. As a primarily Latiru community,
  all communications
will  be in English  and Spanish.

BACKGROUND:  The City received the US EPA Communitywide  Brownfields  Assessment
Grant in October 2022. The grant requires that the City Council receives
  quarterly briefings on the
project's progress. In addition, City staff regularly updates US EPA Region
  9 field staff regarding
the status of the grant. The grant kick-off was held in May 2023 and
  a handful of community
outreach have beenheld at City events. The period ofthe Grant is from
  Octoberl, 2022, to October
31, 2025.

 ANALYSIS:  The  City  Council  approved  Contract  for  a 5-year  term.  The  Contract  stipulated
service  fees in the amount  of $3,435,809,  annually,  for the first  three years  and an annual  CPI
increase  in Years  4 and 5. The Contract  also stipulated  the term  may be extended  two  years by
the parties.

The  Contract  was  awarded  in  2019  before  the  COVID  epidemic  it  world-wide.  NES  has
advised  the City  that COVID  and recent  inflation  has impacted  NES's  operating  costs. On March
7, 2023, NES  submitted  a request  for a monthly  increase  of $6,281 or $75,372, aru'iually,  starting
April  2023.  NES  cited rising  wages,  insurance  premiums,  fuel, vehicle/equipment  parts and other
overhead  costs,  causing  an increase  in operational  expenses  in post COVID  that could  not have
been  foreseen  when  the bid  for  the Contract  was  submitted  in late 2018.  The  increase  being
requested  represents  additional  labor  costs the company  has incurred  to remain  competitive  with
other trades,  according  to NES.

Staff  is not recommending  the approval  of the initial  labor  costs adjustment  and term  extension
requested  by  NES.  Staff  has, instead,  negotiated  the labor  adjustment  sought  by NES  to be
recovered  over  a four-year  period.  Since  the four-year  period  exceeds  the time  period  in the
Contract,  staff  is recommending  a term  extension  to allow  for recovery  to occur  and for NES  to
ensure  it has the ability  to maintain  the vehicles  it uses in the City.  The extension  should  allow
for  industry  commercial  banking  to  sufficiently  finance  those  investments  without  :turther
consideration  upon the City.

The proposed  financial  terms would  do the following:

  1.  Establish  a minimum  Consumer  Price  Index  (CPI)  adjustment  of 3% that NES  would
  receive  annually  moving  forward  through  the term.  If the actual  CPI is greater  than the
  3% minimum  up to a maximum  of 8%, then NES  would  receive  an adjustment  based on
  the actual  CPI.  Staff  is also clarifying  that we should  be using  the month  of August  to
  determine  the CPI adjustment  that would  become  effective  on October  ls', of any given
  year.  The federal  government  typically  releases  the CPI  calculation  about  30-days  after
  the  end  of  the  month  it was  collected.  In  this  case,  August  would  be published  in
  September  of any given  year.  This  would  apply  in Year  5 of the Contract,  as well  as in
  Years  Six through  Twelve  (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12), annually,  for the Contract  extension.

  2.  In  addition,  to  adjust  for  NES's  unforeseen  labor  increases,  NES  would  receive  an

  additional  3%, annually,  in Years  Five  through  Eight  (5, 6, 7, and 8) beyond  the annual
  CPI  adjustment  described  above.  This  would  not be counted  against  the maximum  8%
  that  would  be allowed  in the CPI.  Starting  in Year  Nine  (9), the only  adjustment  that
  would  be permitted  is the annual  CPI, as noted above.

  3.  Finally,  to accommodate  the financial  adjustment,  and to ensure  NES  can reasonably
  obtain  commercial  financing  on  their  equipment,  the  term  is being  proposed  to be
  adjusted  from  ending  on September  30, 2024, to ending  on September  30, 2031.

BACKGROUND:  The Public Works Department provides street sweeping through NES.
Street sweeping services include sweeping of streets, alleyways, parking lots, for special events
and emergency  services.

The City Council approved Contract No. 3542 with NES on July 9, 2019, for an amount
estimated not-to-exceed $3,435,809. The City Council had approved the need to seek proposals
a:[ter a consultant had reviewed whether it would be more cost effective to continue providing the
service in-house or via a third parly. The consultant's analysis showed it would be more cost
effective to contract out the service.

On September 8, 2020, the City Council approved Amendment No. l to Contract No. 3542
which adjusted the CPI for Year 5 of the Contract, modified the termination clause, and added
Columbus Day and Veterans Day to the non-street sweeping  schedule. The RFP required the
Contract to include a CPI adjustment in Year 5; however, it was inadvertently excluded from the
Contract. As such, Amendment No. 1 added a CPI adjustment  for Year 5.

Also, the termination clause within the Contract permitted the City to terminate the Contract  at
any point during the 5-year period. Amendment No. l to Contract No. 3542 modified the
termination clause to give consideration to the substantial investment NES had made in the
purchasing the new street sweeping equipment to meet the Contract obligations. The current
termination clause stipulates the City may not terminate the Contract for convenience during the
first two (2) years but may terminate the Contract for reasons of performance issues and can
terminate the Contract in Years 3, 4 and 5, without cause. Additional holidays were added to
avoid impacting street parking when residents are home for the holidays.

On September 27, 2022, the City Council approved Amendment No. 2 to Contract No. 3542 to
incorporate Park Place and Park Avenue streets into the Contract at no additional cost to the
City.

Street sweeping services are paid primarily by a fee assessed and included in the City's water
customer utility bill. The fee amount is fixed and cannot be changed without going through a
Proposition 218 hearing. Historically,  the fee revenue has been about $710,000, annually. The
remaining cost for the service is paid through special revenue funds such as Measure W funds.

DEFINITIONS

When the following  terms  ue  used in this  Request  for  Proposals,  they  have  the following
meanmg:

  1.  Proposal  item  - Individual  items of work  in the Contractor's  proposal  at an agreed price
  for the work.
  2.  Curb  Mile  - A curb mile  equals  5,280  feet and is the measurement  used to designate
  those  miles predetcrmined  by City to be swept by the street sweeping  Contractor.
  3.  Debris  -  All  litter,  rubbish,  organic  debris  including  leaves  and grass clippings,  sand,
  dirt,  garbage  and  other  foreign  material  removable  from  a paved  street  with  a
  mechanical  street sweeper.
  4.  Emergency  (As-needed)  Services  -  Sweeping  required  by  City  excluding  regularly
  scheduled  street  sweeping  that requires  additional  dedicated  labor,  equipment  and work
  hours.  Billing  for emergency  sweeps will  be based on an hourly  rate with  travel  time
  excluded,
  5.  Fully  Operational  -  In  a  condition  to  undertake  the  function  to  adequately
  complete  sweeping  schedules.
  6.  Inclement  Weather  -  Weather  conditions  that  prohibit  the  effective  operation  of
  sweeping  operations,  such as heavy rain or winds.
  7.  Non-emergency  Sweeps  -  Sweeping  required  by  City  excluding  regularly  scheduled
  street  sweeping  that  requires  additional  dedicated  labor,  equipment  and work  hours.
  Billing  for non-emergency  sweeps  will  be based  on an hourly  rate  with  travel  time
  excluded.
  8.  Parking  Lots  - Asphalt,  concrete  or other hard surfaced  areas primarily  for the parking
  of automobiles.
  9.  Periodic  Inspection  -  Routinely  scheduled  or randomly  noticed  inspection  or audit
  conducted  by City.
  10. Quality  of Sweeping  - The street sweeper  shall leave designated  areas of sweeping  free
  of  all dirt, litter,  debris,  and visual  dust.

EXISTING  OPERATION

The City is located in the Gateway Cities region of southeastern Los Angeles County with an
estimated current population of 98,633. It is the 17' largest city in the County, located 7 miles
from Downtown Los Angcles. The City covers an area of approximately  7.5 square miles.

The City's street sweeping operation is managed by the Street and Sewer Division of the Public
Works Department. Sweeping services are currently provided by City employees and utilizing its
own equipment. The City is seeking to provide these services through a contract with a sweeping
contractor.

The City has approximately  125 miles of streets, 12 miles of alleys, or an equivalent of 17,976
lane miles per year. In addition, there are approximately  1,500 lane miles per year of street
medians. Residential  streets are swept during daytime hours once per week. Commercial,
indushial streets, school areas, and alleys are swept at night once per week. Street medians are
swept two times a week at night. Sweeping services are perfomied on all holidays. Exhibit A -
Part 2, Table 1 shows the approximate route miles for the City's street sweeping program.

Sweeping is coordinated with refuse collection, which is provided pursuant to an agreement with
Waste Management Inc., the City's waste hauler, Waste Management Inc., collects the sweeping
debris deposited at the transfer station located at 9599 Salt Lake Avenue, South Gate 90280 at no
charge, This arrangement is expected to continue.  The street sweeper, to the extent possible,
follows the refuse collection vehicle. Each year, the City provides sweeping support to three
special events. All events require a pre-event sweep and post-event sweep to remove debris. For
costing purpose, City has included a three additional events to the list, which is to be determined
in the future.

Residential strcets have posted parking restrictions of four (4) hours, between 7:30 am and 4:30
pm. Cars are required to be removed from streets during those time periods posted for street
sweeping. Parking enforcement personnel follow the sweepers and cite vehicles that obsttuct
street sweeping efforts. The successful contractor will coordinate with the Police Department on
routing and service delivery to ensure effective enforcement.

The City is interested in making improvements  to its existing program by reducing parking
restrictions in residential neighborhoods  from four hours to two hours. The City expects the
successful Contractor to formulate and implement the changes. Revised parking restrictions will
require the selected Contractor  to purchase and install new signage in the residential
neighborhoods.  As described in Exhibit A, some of the signage materials currently in possession

CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

CALL TO ORDER  Maria del Pilar Avalos, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to
  order to 6:38 p.m.

INVOCATION  Steve Costley, Director of Parks & Recreation
PLEDGE OF
ALLEGIANCE  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Resources

ROLL CALL  Sonia Guerrero, Recording Secretary

PRESENT  Mayor Maria del Pilar Avalos, Vice Mayor Gil Hurtado, Council Member
  Joshua Barron, Council Member Maria Davila, and Council Member Al
  Rios; City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Chris Jeffers, City
  Attorney Raul F. Salinas

LATE  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk arrived at 7:03 p.m.

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  unanimously approved items A & B by motion of Council Member Rios
  and seconded by Council Member Davila.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Barron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes; Mayor Avalos,
  yes.

  a.  Resolution No. 2023-60-CC entitled Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, California, approving the
  Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Consolidated Annual Performance and
  Evaluation Report (CAPER); and

  b.  Authorized the City Manager, or designee, to submit to the U.S.
  Department of Housing and Urban Development the City's FY
  2022-2023 CAPER.

  Meredith Elguira, the Director of Community Development, introduced
  Housing Manager Carol Averall.

  Ms. Averell explains that the purpose of this report is to provide
  information on the closing of the fiscal year and an evaluation of the
  report. The report covers the accomplishments of the CDBG and home-
  funded projects for the year 2022-2023. This year, the city was able to
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT'D  assist one business with commercial rehabilitation. While also assisting
  three hundred and fifty-three direct client services that included
  discrimination allegations and landlord/tenant counseling sessions were
  provided via the Fair Housing Foundation. Eleven thousand nine hundred
  fifty-six graffiti abatement assignments were completed, and staff
  responded to two thousand one hundred and thirty-eight calls. She also
  wanted to mention that they were able to assist one hundred and fifty-six
  people via CDBG-CV funded public service activities for college
  internships through the CLLI, Family Violence Program, and Police
  Explore Program through the South Gate Police Department, Rental and
  Utility Assistance through HVC and assistive technology and minor home
  modifications were provided by the Southern California Resource Service
  for Independent Living. She lastly covered some recommendations, such
  as adopting a resolution to receive and approve the Program year 2022-
  2023 CAPER and authorizing the City Manager to submit the CAPER to
  the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

  Mayor Avalos asked if anyone in the audience and zoom wished to speak
  on this item.

  Mario Dominguez first wanted to ask why there were so many zeros on
  the chart provided by Ms. Averell. He also expressed that the city should
  do a better job of notifying the public that the city has programs to assist
  the residents. He shared that he wanted to apply for a program for housing
  improvement program but was unable to due to the fact that the value of
  the property cannot surpass six hundred thousand.

  Having no one else come forward, Mayor Avalos closed the audience
  portion.

  Ms. Averell responds to Mr. Dominquez's concerns regarding the chart
  shared. She explains that no units were developed this year, so there was
  nothing to report in value.

  Council Member Barron asked if Ms. Averell could go over what
  programs the city is developing to change the numbers hopefully reported.

  Ms. Averell shared that the city is currently in the process of working on
  an affordable housing unit for sale for low-income families. They are also
  working with Habitats for Humanity. Two of those units are for rent, and
  twelve will be for sale.

  Council Member Barron explained that he truly believes that the program
  will be able to assist community members with affordable housing and
  thanked Ms. Averell for the information provided in the presentation.

  Page 2 of 11
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT'D  Council Member Rios asked Ms. Averell if she could briefly discuss job
  opportunities and if anyone benefited from these programs.

  Ms. Averell explained that the Helpline Youth Counseling received CDBG
  coronavirus funding to cover the rent for many of the families that were
  not able to afford it. They are also working with ARPA funds.

  Council Member Rios asked if any funding occurred for job opportunities.

  Ms. Elguria responded to Council Member Rios question and explained
  that no funding was provided for job training programs last year. However,
  funding was provided to an internship program. That is something that
  they are exploring next year.

  Mayor Avalos wanted to clarify Mr. Dominguez's comment on the house
  renovation program that if your property exceeds the value of six hundred
  thousand, you do not qualify. She asked if that applies to the land or the
  building itself. Many of our properties in the city fall into a category in
  which the property land exceeds the value, but the actual building is
  delipidated.

  Ms. Averell explains that the program requires the property to be evaluated
  before a loan can be given. If we look at the property value that exceeds
  the value of six hundred thousand and the city grants a loan of fifty
  thousand, then the property will not qualify because it falls out of the
  threshold of six hundred and thirty thousand. She also explains that she
  spoke personally with Mr. Dominguez about a program for senior citizens
  in which they will be able to gain assistance on home improvements.

  Mayor Avalos wanted to clarify that this is a separate program.

  Ms. Averell responded yes.

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE (NON-AGENDA
ITEMS)  Olivia Mora, 5246 Wood Ave, claims that her landlord authorized the city
  to inspect the property without the tenant knowing and then proceeded to
  give the tenant the eviction letter. The tenant claims the electrical panel
  went out, leaving her and her family without electricity. She claims to
  have called the police to assist. Edison responded that the electrical wiring
  was not correctly connected, resulting in a small fire on the property. She
  contacted the Community Development Department for assistance and
  said they informed her that electricity is a luxury and not a necessity. She
  asked the council for assistance.

  Page 3 of 11
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE (NON-AGENDA
ITEMS) CONT'D  Bill Wallace, 8823 Beaudine Ave, noted the last time he attended a
  meeting for a Prop he advocated for. He noted that you could obtain more
  information online. He encouraged fellow residents to participate in the
  Proposition.

  Nicolas Cortuva explained how he works for an organization for tenant
  rights. He noted the importance of having tenant protection. He also
  wanted to commend Ms. Mora for sharing her story.

  Gabriel Guerrero speaks about tenant rights and the injustices of rent
  prices. He asked the council to be compassionate and help those
  requesting rent assistance. He has lived in the city for years and noticed a
  drastic change. He lastly thanked the council for their help.

  Miguel Molteo wanted to speak about tenant protection and healthy
  housing. He is a fellow resident of the city, currently a tenant in the city.
  He feels that code enforcement needs to assist tenants.

  Maria Sandoval asked the council for assistance. She states that there is a
  parking issue. She told David Torres that the city would post no parking
  signs along the streets. Unfortunately, nothing has been done, and people
  continue to park there. She stresses that some vehicles have been parked
  there for the past four months. She would appreciate the council's help
  because these parked cars are bothersome.

  Fellow resident Francisco explains that he has parking issues along his
  street. He spoke to the traffic bureau to address this issue. He also wants to
  discuss the traffic on Firestone Blvd and Imperial Hwy.

  Fellow resident Jose wanted to echo similar concerns about parking on
  Southern. He states that more motorhomes are coming into the city far
  from his property.

  Ashely Esquivel wanted to speak with the council regarding the increased
  monthly payment for the water. She would like to propose a solution for
  this water bill increase. She wants to know the steps to help the residents
  during this time.

  Mario Dominguez wanted to clarify what makes winning a financial report
  so important. He also wanted to know which committees are involved.

  Irma Lopez is from the city of Cudahy. However, she came to the meeting
  to express her concerns about the recent increase in the city. She asks the
  council to help her fellow citizens with some form of rental control.

  Page 4 of 11
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE (NON-AGENDA
ITEMS) CONT'D  Thomas Buckley wanted to echo similar concerns regarding the water bill.

  Ms. Alice disagrees with renter control. She also spoke to the council
  regarding the water bill. She spoke regarding the issues of parking on
  Southern.

  Veronica Sanchez lives in the city of Cudahy. She supports Renters
  Control. She explains that people like herself who live from paycheck to
  paycheck struggle the most. She stresses assistance from the council.

  Betty Sanchez also came in to support the renter's control. She explains
  that times have changed, and many cannot purchase a home. She hopes the
  council can help with some form of rental control.

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS  Meredith Elguira, Director of Community Development, responded to Ms.
  Mora's concerns. She explains that the code enforcement department is
  addressing the issue.

  Mayor Avalos requested specific resources, such as phone numbers for the
  appropriate departments, to help assist her during this time.

  Mayor Avalos thanked Mr. Wallace for sharing and encouraging fellow
  residents of the Proposition.

  Mayor Avalos asked Mr. Cervantes if he had any update on this issue. She
  is aware that Ms. Sanchez has come in for this issue prior.

  Chris Jeffers, City Manager, explains that some parts of Southern, the city
  does not own. Many of those areas are owned by the Department of Water
  and Power.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado explains that this is a recurring issue along
  Independence. He also notes that there is illegal dumping that is occurring.

  Council Member Barron wanted to echo similar concerns. He explains
  how it can be a burden on our street.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado continued by asking if there was some form of
  conversation occurring or if there was a status with the Department of
  Light and Water.

  Wendy 0' Kelly, Finance Director, addressed the recent concerns
  regarding the water bill.

  Page 5 of 11
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT'D  Mr. Jeffers stated that the city has provided assistance for residents who
  needed it regarding their utility bills.

  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer, wanted to echo concerns of the water
  billing and the shift in price increase and decrease.

  Captain Perez addressed the parking situation and what they are doing to
  help resolve it.

  Arturo Cervantez, Director of Public Works, explained the traffic signal
  synchronization program and why there is a challenge in certain parts of
  the city.

  Mayor Avalos stated that the issue of rent control will not be discussed at
  this time.

  Ms. 0' Kelly went over the LIHWAP program and the covid relief credit.

  Mr. Cervantez provided an update on the capital improvement projects
  going on around the city.

  Steve Costley, Interim Director of Parks and Recreation described the
  Glow Party at South Gate Park. He also went over upcoming events
  happening in the city.

  Ms. Elguira encouraged residents to provide Community Development
  input and the active outreaches happening.

  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk, explained the reasoning for her late arrival and
  had nothing else to report.

  Mr. De La Paz had nothing to report.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Resources, went over the positions that
  are available to apply for.

  Mr. Perez provided an update on new police officers joining South Gate
  Police Department.

  Mr. Jeffers reminded the public of a zoom meeting regarding an update on
  the Tweedy Mile Project.

  Raul F. Salinas, City Attorney, recognized the loss of former Mayor
  William De Witt.

  Page 6 of 11
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 12, 2023

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT'D  Council Member Davila attended the Glow Party at South Gate Park and
  enjoyed seeing a lot of teenagers having a great time. She also recognized
  the loss of Mr. De Witt.

  Council Member Barron commended code enforcement in addressing an
  issue that a resident had. He also wanted to remind residents about the
  monthly newsletter. He stated there are still gift cards available for use
  around the city and new businesses that just opened. He also wanted to
  bring awareness to theft and fraud being more prevalent for the elderly
  population.

  Council Member Rios recognized the loss of Mr. De Witt and provided
  events happening at ELAC and around the city.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado asked if it was possible for South Gate to have their
  own school district. He also addressed people's concerns on rent control.
  He echoes recognition for the loss of Mr. De Witt.

  Mayor Avalos also spoke some words describing Mr. De Witt and
  remembrance of 9/11. She also reminded the audience of submitting name
  ideas for the West Santa Ana Branch and welcomed students going back to
  school.

CONSENT CALENDAR  Agenda Items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 were approved by motion of

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Barron, yes; Council Member Davila,
